events/founding-of-constantinople-330/su: Constantine refounded Byzantium as 'New Rome', dedicated on 11 May 330, with churches such as Holy Apostles. Its bishop would rise to second rank after Rome (381) and become the Ecumenical Patriarch, centre of Byzantine Orthodoxy for over a thousand years.
events/founding-of-constantinople-330/ca: Strategic need for an eastern capital
events/founding-of-constantinople-330/co: Rivalry between Old and New Rome
events/conversion-of-ethiopia-aksum-330/: Conversion of the kingdom of Aksum

Frumentius, a Syrian Christian captured as a youth and raised at the Aksumite court, was consecrated bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria and returned to evangelise. King Ezana's coins shift from pagan crescent-and-disc to the cross around 340, making Aksum one of the first Christian states.
Red Sea trade and Christian merchants
Ethiopian church dependent on Alexandria for its bishop (abuna) until 1959
events/conversion-of-georgia-337/summary: Georgian tradition holds that Nino, a captive woman from Cappadocia, healed Queen Nana and converted King Mirian III of Kartli, who adopted Christianity around 326–337. Rufinus records the story within decades. The Svetitskhoveli cathedral at Mtskheta marks the site.
events/conversion-of-georgia-337/causes/: Influence of Roman and Armenian Christianity
events/conversion-of-georgia-337/consequ: Georgian script and literature developed for Christian texts
events/persecution-of-shapur-ii-340/titl: Great persecution of Persian Christians under Shapur II
events/persecution-of-shapur-ii-340/summ: After Rome became Christian, the Sasanian king Shapur II treated his Christian subjects as potential traitors and imposed a double tax. The catholicos Simeon bar Sabbae refused to collect it and was executed around 344; thousands of martyrs followed over forty years.
events/persecution-of-shapur-ii-340/caus: Constantine's letter to Shapur as patron of Christians
events/persecution-of-shapur-ii-340/cons: Martyr Acts of the Persian church
Church of the East's careful distancing from Roman church politics
events/ulfilas-mission-to-goths-341/titl: Ulfilas consecrated bishop for the Goths
events/ulfilas-mission-to-goths-341/summ: Ulfilas (Wulfila), of Cappadocian captive descent, was consecrated bishop by Eusebius of Nicomedia and evangelised the Goths, inventing a Gothic alphabet to translate the Bible. Because his theology was Homoian, the Germanic peoples who followed the Goths were largely 'Arian' Christians for two centuries.
events/ulfilas-mission-to-goths-341/cons: Homoian Christianity among Goths, Vandals and Lombards
events/edict-of-thessalonica-380/summary: Emperor Theodosius I decreed that all peoples should hold the faith of Damasus of Rome and Peter of Alexandria — Nicene Trinitarianism — branding others heretics. Nicene Christianity thus became the official religion of the empire.
events/edict-of-thessalonica-380/consequ: Legal suppression of heresy and later paganism
Union of orthodoxy and imperial law
events/council-of-constantinople-381/sum: Called by Theodosius, about 150 eastern bishops reaffirmed Nicaea, condemned Homoian and Pneumatomachian teaching and confessed the Holy Spirit 'the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified'. The resulting Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed is the most widely used Christian creed.
events/council-of-constantinople-381/lon: By 381 the Cappadocian Fathers — Basil (d. 379), Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa — had clarified the vocabulary of one ousia (essence) in three hypostases, allowing many who had hesitated over homoousios to accept Nicaea. The council, presided over first by Meletius of Antioch and then briefly by Gregory of Nazianzus (who resigned amid factional disputes), confirmed the Nicene faith and affirmed the full deity of the Holy Spirit without using homoousios for the Spirit. Its third canon gave Constantinople 'the prerogative of honour after the Bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome' — a claim Rome long resisted. The creed associated with it was formally recognised at Chalcedon in 451. The later Western addition of 'and the Son' (Filioque) to its article on the Spirit became a central Catholic–Orthodox dispute. Nontrinitarian bodies regard the creed as philosophical development; Trinitarian churches see it as safeguarding biblical worship of Father, Son and Spirit.
events/council-of-constantinople-381/con: End of imperial support for Arianism in the East
events/jerome-vulgate-382/summary: Commissioned by Pope Damasus to revise the Latin Gospels, Jerome later settled in Bethlehem and translated most of the Old Testament from Hebrew. His Vulgate became the standard Latin Bible of the Western church for a thousand years and was declared authentic by Trent.
events/jerome-vulgate-382/consequences/1: Debates on Hebrew vs Septuagint canon
events/council-of-carthage-397/title: Council of Carthage and the biblical canon
events/council-of-carthage-397/summary: Repeating the Synod of Hippo (393), the Council of Carthage listed the books of Scripture, including the 27 books of the New Testament and an Old Testament with the books Protestants call deuterocanonical or apocrypha. Augustine took part. It was a regional decision, confirmed by later African and Roman acts.
events/council-of-carthage-397/causes/0: Need for a fixed public reading list
events/council-of-carthage-397/consequen: Western canon later reaffirmed at Florence and Trent
Reference point for Catholic–Protestant canon debates
events/armenian-alphabet-405/title: Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet
events/armenian-alphabet-405/summary: With Catholicos Sahak and King Vramshapuh's support, Mesrop Mashtots devised an alphabet so the Armenian people could read Scripture and liturgy in their own tongue. The Bible translation that followed launched a golden age of Armenian literature.
events/armenian-alphabet-405/causes/0: Christian worship in Greek and Syriac not understood by the people
events/synod-of-seleucia-ctesiphon-410/t: Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon organises the Persian church
events/synod-of-seleucia-ctesiphon-410/s: With the permission of Shah Yazdegerd I, the bishops of Persia met under Catholicos Isaac, accepted the Nicene Creed and organised their church into provinces under the bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon. The synod of 424 under Dadisho later declared the catholicos independent of 'Western' fathers.
events/synod-of-seleucia-ctesiphon-410/c: Mission of Bishop Marutha of Maypherqat
Structure of the Church of the East
events/sack-of-rome-410/summary: The Visigoths under Alaric, themselves Homoian Christians, sacked Rome for three days in August 410. Pagans blamed the abandonment of the gods; Augustine responded with The City of God, contrasting the earthly and heavenly cities.
events/sack-of-rome-410/consequences/1: Christian reflection on history and empire
events/pelagius-condemned-418/summary: African bishops, led by Augustine's theology, condemned teachings associated with Pelagius and Caelestius: that Adam's sin harmed only himself, that infants are born without original sin, and that grace merely assists free will. Pope Zosimus and Emperor Honorius followed; the Council of Ephesus (431) confirmed the condemnation.
events/pelagius-condemned-418/causes/0: Pelagius' moral reform preaching in Rome
events/pelagius-condemned-418/consequenc: Augustinian doctrine of original sin and grace in the West
events/council-of-ephesus-431/summary: Convoked by Theodosius II, the council led by Cyril of Alexandria deposed Nestorius of Constantinople, who had objected to calling Mary Theotokos ('God-bearer'), and affirmed the single subject of the incarnate Word. John of Antioch's party held a rival meeting; a Formula of Reunion followed in 433. Churches of the Syriac East never accepted the condemnation of Nestorius.
events/council-of-ephesus-431/longText: The controversy turned on how to speak of Christ's unity. Nestorius, trained in the Antiochene tradition that stressed the full and distinct humanity of Christ, preferred 'Christotokos' to 'Theotokos', fearing the latter confused the divine and human. Cyril of Alexandria saw in this a division of Christ into two sons and insisted that the eternal Word himself was born, suffered and died in the flesh; Mary is therefore Mother of God. Cyril opened the council on 22 June 431 before the Antiochene bishops arrived and deposed Nestorius; John of Antioch's party, arriving days later, deposed Cyril. The emperor eventually upheld Nestorius' deposition and he died in exile in Egypt. The 433 Formula of Reunion — 'a union of two natures' — reconciled Cyril and John. The council is recognised as the Third Ecumenical Council by Catholic, Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox churches. The Church of the East, which venerated Theodore of Mopsuestia, never accepted it and is often (inaccurately, in its own view) called 'Nestorian'; a 1994 Common Christological Declaration with Rome acknowledged a shared faith expressed in different terms.
events/council-of-ephesus-431/consequenc: Theotokos affirmed and Marian devotion strengthened
Estrangement of the Church of the East
events/patrick-mission-to-ireland-432/su: Patrick, a Romano-British Christian once enslaved in Ireland, returned as bishop and evangelised the north, as his Confession recounts. The traditional date of 432 is uncertain; Palladius had been sent by Pope Celestine in 431. Irish monastic Christianity later sent missionaries across Europe.
events/patrick-mission-to-ireland-432/co: Celtic missions to Scotland, England and the continent
events/robber-council-of-ephesus-449/sum: Presided over by Dioscorus of Alexandria, the council rehabilitated the monk Eutyches, deposed Flavian of Constantinople (who died soon after) and refused to read Leo's Tome. Leo called it a latrocinium ('robbery'); Oriental Orthodox churches regard its condemnation as unjust to Dioscorus.
events/robber-council-of-ephesus-449/con: Council of Chalcedon called to reverse it
events/council-of-chalcedon-451/summary: Some 520 bishops, summoned by Emperor Marcian, deposed Dioscorus of Alexandria, received Leo's Tome and defined Christ as one person 'acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'. Canon 28 raised Constantinople to near-parity with Rome. The definition was rejected by most Christians of Egypt, Syria and Armenia, producing the first lasting division of the church.
events/council-of-chalcedon-451/longText: Chalcedon sought to close the debate left open after Ephesus by holding together the Alexandrian insistence on one incarnate Word and the Antiochene concern for two complete natures. Its definition borrowed from Cyril's letters, Leo's Tome and the Formula of Reunion, confessing one and the same Son, perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, 'in two natures'. For its defenders — Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and most Protestants — it is a balanced boundary marking out heresies on both sides. For the Miaphysite (often called Monophysite by opponents) churches of Egypt, Syria, Armenia and Ethiopia, 'in two natures' sounded Nestorian and betrayed Cyril's formula 'one incarnate nature of God the Word'; they regarded the deposition of Dioscorus as political, the work of Rome and Constantinople. Imperial attempts at reconciliation (the Henotikon of 482, Justinian's council of 553, Monoenergism and Monothelitism in the 7th century) failed, and separate hierarchies emerged through figures like Severus of Antioch and Jacob Baradaeus. Many historians now see the dispute as partly terminological and bound up with language, regional identity and imperial politics. Agreed statements between Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox theologians (1989–1990) and between Rome and individual Oriental churches have affirmed a common faith in Christ expressed in different formulas.
events/council-of-chalcedon-451/conseque: Separation of the Oriental Orthodox churches
